summary: Describes private SIP header fields used by 3GPP for purposes such as charging and information about networks a call passes through, along with their limited applicability. It obsoletes RFC 3455.

eli5.summary: Phone networks write extra notes on call messages for billing and tracking. This lists the notes and where they should be used.

subtitle: Six private SIP header fields that 3GPP networks use for identity, roaming, access details and charging, and why they are not for the open Internet.

tldr.problem: 3GPP uses SIP in its IP Multimedia Subsystem, and its networks needed things plain SIP did not offer: telling a user which address a call was meant for, naming the visited network, describing the access network, and tying charging records together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six private header fields, each starting with P-, and for each one says where it applies, who may add it and who must remove it. The fields assume trust between the networks that handle the message.
tldr.outcome: The headers are for private, trusted networks only and are not appropriate for the Internet. RFC 7315 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 3455 and has since been updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 7315 is an Informational RFC published in July 2014. It obsoletes RFC 3455 and has been updated by RFC 7913, RFC 7976 and RFC 9878.

sections.title: Private Headers for 3GPP Networks
sections.content:
The 3GPP uses the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) to set up and tear down multimedia sessions in its IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS). RFC 3455 defined the SIP private header extensions, called P-headers, that the 3GPP specification needs. RFC 7315 obsoletes it and updates the descriptions to cover additional requirements of 3GPP Release 11.

The applicability is narrow. The extensions assume certain network topologies, a link between SIP and the lower layers, and transitive trust. The RFC says these assumptions hold only in private networks and that the headers are not appropriate for use in an Internet environment. Each header gets its own applicability statement that spells out the conditions.

The RFC defines six header fields. The 3GPP requirements behind them are written down in RFC 4083.
sections.eli5: These are special sticky notes that phone networks put on call messages. They only work when the networks trust each other, so they are not meant for the whole Internet.

sections.title: Registration and Called-Party Headers
sections.content:
P-Associated-URI is added by a registrar to the 200 (OK) response to a REGISTER request. It lists the other URIs that the service provider has associated with the registered address-of-record, so the user agent learns which identities it may use, for example in the From header field. A client must not assume those associated URIs are registered. If an address-of-record has no associated URIs, the header is left out. Proxies must pass it on unchanged.

P-Called-Party-ID solves a different problem. A user may have a business and a personal SIP URI, both registered. When the home proxy retargets an incoming INVITE to the contact address the user registered, the original Request-URI is lost. The To header cannot fill the gap, because it is set by the caller and may name someone else after forwarding.

So the proxy copies the Request-URI it received into a P-Called-Party-ID header before retargeting. The called user agent can then play a distinctive ring or filter calls depending on which URI was dialled. A user agent must not insert this header, and a proxy must not insert it in REGISTER requests. The RFC notes that the History-Info header in RFC 7044 gives equivalent coverage, but P-Called-Party-ID is used entirely inside the 3GPP system.
sections.eli5: If you have two mailboxes, a work one and a home one, a note on each letter tells you which mailbox it came out of. P-Called-Party-ID is that note for phone calls.

sections.title: Visited Network and Access Network Headers
sections.content:
P-Visited-Network-ID tells the home network which visited network is serving a roaming user. A proxy in the visited network may add a text string or token that the home network knows, and the home network can check that a roaming agreement exists before authorising the registration. The identifier must be globally unique, and the RFC suggests drawing it from the network's DNS domain name. A user agent must not insert it. A home-network proxy must delete it when forwarding outside the home network, to protect privacy. Because other proxies could alter it, intermediaries must use hop-by-hop integrity protection such as IPsec.

P-Access-Network-Info carries details about how the user agent reaches the network, such as the radio access technology and the radio cell identity. The serving proxy can use this to tune services, for example localised services based on cell ID. The RFC notes the information is potentially very sensitive. It must not be sent in an initial unauthenticated, unprotected request such as REGISTER, and the proxy must strip it before sending the message to an untrusted domain. A proxy must not modify the value, and must remove any value marked network-provided when sending to an untrusted entity.
sections.eli5: One note says which company's tower your phone is borrowing while you travel. Another says what kind of connection you are using. Both stay inside the family of trusted networks.

sections.title: Charging Headers
sections.content:
P-Charging-Function-Addresses tells each proxy in a transaction where to send charging records. It names up to two addresses for each of two kinds of function: the Charging Collection Function (ccf, ccf-2) for offline charging such as postpaid accounts, and the Event Charging Function (ecf, ecf-2) for online charging such as prepaid accounts. Implementations try the first address, and must use the second if the first is not available. A proxy must remove the header when the next hop is outside its administrative domain. The charging records themselves are usually not sent with SIP.

P-Charging-Vector carries the information needed to correlate charging records produced by different entities for the same session. Its mandatory parameter is icid-value, the IMS Charging Identity, which must be globally unique. Other parameters include icid-generated-at, the originating and terminating inter-operator identifiers (orig-ioi, term-ioi), one or more transit-ioi values for networks in between (a transit network can appear as void if policy hides its name), and related-icid for linking call legs of the same remote-end dialog.

Only one instance of each charging header may appear in a request or response. Applications using P-Charging-Vector within their own applicability may define extra parameters without going through the IETF process.
sections.eli5: These notes are like a receipt number stapled to a phone call. Every company that helps carry the call writes down the same number, so the bill can be put together correctly later.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
Every header depends on trust, and the RFC treats each one separately. P-Associated-URI is not very sensitive but could leak a user's list of identities, so it should be used where SIP messages are encrypted. P-Called-Party-ID raises no significant concern, although an eavesdropper could collect registered identities. P-Visited-Network-ID, P-Charging-Function-Addresses and P-Charging-Vector must be protected hop by hop with integrity protection such as IPsec, because an untrusted entity in the path could swap values or disturb charging correlation.

P-Access-Network-Info is the most sensitive, since it can carry the cell ID. It must not be sent outside the 3GPP domain, and any proxy in the private trust domain is required to delete it before forwarding outside. A rogue user agent that sends false access information can do no more harm than keep the user from certain services.
sections.eli5: Because these notes can reveal where you are or how you are billed, they must be kept inside a locked group of trusted companies. Anyone outside that group must not see them.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 3455
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the differences from RFC 3455. The main points are:

  • Proxies do not add, read, modify or delete P-Associated-URI, which the new text states explicitly.
  • The relationship between P-Called-Party-ID and History-Info is acknowledged.
  • New rules cover user agents inside the private network, such as gateways, for both charging headers.
  • P-Access-Network-Info gains many new access technology values (for example several IEEE 802.11, IEEE 802.3 and DSL variants), the value 3GPP-CDMA2000 is replaced by three 3GPP2 values, and proxies may add network-provided values.
  • Applications may define extra P-Charging-Vector parameters, and P-Called-Party-ID may now appear in PUBLISH.
sections.eli5: This is the list of fixes and additions compared with the older version, like a new edition of a rulebook with a page of what is different.
